item.title: Every door has a lock and an owner: governing third-party access for a Japanese online securities firm
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Japanese online securities firm can govern vendor access to its cloud and machines: an access ledger, narrow roles, behaviour alerts and a per-vendor kill switch.
item.content:encoded:
A Japanese online securities firm ran on AWS and relied on a long list of suppliers: a data platform, an observability vendor, a managed service provider for office devices, SaaS tools connected to its email and files. Each had been given access when it was onboarded, and nobody had a single view of who could reach what. When attackers used one data platform's trusted access to raid its customers' AWS accounts, the firm set out to know, narrow, watch and be able to cut every supplier's access.

The situation

A Japanese online securities firm ran its trading and account platforms on AWS. Over the years it had connected a long list of suppliers: a data platform that read market and customer data through a cross-account role, an observability vendor with read access to logs and metrics, a managed service provider that ran remote management agents on office devices, and SaaS tools connected to the firm's email and file storage through OAuth grants. Each connection had been approved by the team that needed it, at the time it was needed. Nobody had a complete list.

The FSA's cybersecurity guidelines for the financial sector, in effect since October 2024, treat third-party risk management as a core area, including outsourcing and cloud services5. The firm's supplier assessments were thorough on paper: questionnaires, certifications and contract clauses. What they did not show was what each supplier could technically do inside the firm's systems today.

Why now. In early November 2026, Wiz reported that an attacker had used credentials tied to Qubole's AWS account to assume integration roles that customers had created to trust Qubole, then collected secrets and data from those customers' accounts1. Days later, N-able took its hosted N-central remote management platform offline after a researcher published alleged zero-days2. Both showed the same thing: a supplier's access is only as safe as the supplier.

What had to be true

  • Known: every supplier's technical access in one ledger.
  • Owned: an internal owner and a business reason for each.
  • Narrow: each supplier can do only what its service needs.
  • Watched: unusual supplier activity raises an alert.
  • Revocable: any supplier's access can be cut quickly, without guesswork.
  • Evidenced: supervisors and auditors can see all of the above.

Architecture

Every cross-account role was rebuilt following AWS's guidance for third-party access: a trust policy naming the vendor's account, a unique external ID for the relationship and permissions limited to the specific actions and resources the service needed34. Service control policies set limits no supplier role could exceed, such as never reading the secrets manager or changing identity settings. Where a vendor could commit to fixed source networks, resource policies only accepted vendor access from those networks. The model is the one Kubernetes teaches for role-based access: a narrowly defined role, bound explicitly to named identities6.

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: when the supplier itself is compromised

External IDs are not enough. An external ID protects against the confused deputy problem, where one customer tricks a vendor into acting on someone else's account3. It does not help when the vendor's own systems are compromised; in the Qubole case, the attacker's requests were accepted by customers' roles1. So the firm assumed every supplier could one day be the attacker, and designed so that a compromised supplier could reach only a narrow slice of data, could not read secrets and would trigger alerts by behaving differently.

Detecting "normal but wrong". A compromised supplier uses valid credentials, so authentication alerts stay quiet. The firm built a simple baseline per supplier: usual source networks, usual hours, usual API actions and usual data volumes. Departures from that baseline, such as a new network, listing every bucket or reading parameters it had never read, raised alerts to the security team and the supplier's internal owner.

Remote management tools. The managed service provider's agents could run commands on every office device, so they received the strictest treatment: access only to office devices, never to trading systems; just-in-time sessions approved per task; and a tested way to stop the agents across the fleet if the provider was compromised. See the MSP cyber resilience case study.

Assume every supplier will one day be breached. Design so that day costs you a narrow slice of data and an alert, not your whole estate.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Technical ledger of access, not only questionnairesRely on supplier assessmentsShows what suppliers can actually do today
Assume supplier compromiseTrust certified suppliersValid credentials are exactly what attackers use
Guardrails no vendor role can exceedCareful role design onlyOne mistake in a role does not expose everything
Behaviour alerts per supplierGeneric anomaly detectionSmall baselines are cheap and catch "normal but wrong"
Just-in-time remote managementAlways-on agent accessLimits what a compromised provider can do at any moment
Rehearsed per-vendor revocationRevoke when neededCutting access in a crisis needs a known, safe procedure

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with the inventory of roles trusting outside accounts. It found integrations for services the firm had stopped using years earlier, still active. Differently: involve procurement from the start, so new suppliers are onboarded into the ledger rather than discovered later. Related: the 10 November tech news, the machine and agent identity case study, securing MCP servers and where I work.

If you cannot list every supplier that can reach your cloud, or cut one off quickly, see my fractional CTO work, or analyse your challenge and bring the result to a call.

item.title: One GPU, many models: consolidating small AI models for an Indian multilingual marketplace
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an Indian multilingual marketplace can serve many small AI models without a GPU each: partitioned GPUs, shared base models with adapters and routing by model.
item.content:encoded:
An Indian online marketplace served buyers and sellers in many Indian languages. Behind its search, listings and support sat a growing collection of small AI models: embedding models, rerankers, classifiers and fine-tuned language variants. Each had been given a whole GPU, most of which sat idle. As new GPU partitioning options reached mainstream cloud services, the company set out to serve the same models on far less hardware, without one model's traffic slowing another.

The situation

An Indian online marketplace connected buyers with small and mid-sized sellers across the country, in English and many Indian languages. Over several years its teams had added small AI models wherever they helped: embedding models and rerankers for search in each major language, classifiers for listing quality and support routing, language identification, and fine-tuned language models that helped sellers write listings. Each team had deployed its models independently, and the simplest way to get a model into production had been to give it its own GPU.

The result was a large GPU bill for hardware that was mostly idle. Many models needed only a fraction of a GPU's memory and compute, and traffic followed Indian daily patterns, with quiet nights and sharp peaks around sales. Adding support for another language meant another set of models and, by habit, more GPUs. Finance wanted the bill down; product wanted more languages.

Why now. GPU partitioning was moving into mainstream managed services. AWS added GPU partitioning to SageMaker AI real-time inference, using NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU so one GPU can be split into isolated partitions, each with dedicated compute and memory12. At the same time, reports that Microsoft was winding down rented capacity on older GPUs underlined how quickly hardware choices age5. Using every GPU fully had become a design goal, not an afterthought.

What had to be true

  • Far fewer GPUs for the same models and traffic.
  • No noisy neighbours for latency-critical models such as search.
  • Quality held per language and task after any consolidation.
  • New languages cheap to add, without new hardware by default.
  • Cost visible per model and language, so decisions follow value.
  • Teams still independent: shared infrastructure, not a central bottleneck.

Architecture

We sorted every model into one of three groups. Small, latency-critical models, such as search embeddings and rerankers, went onto Multi-Instance GPU partitions, which give each model its own slice of compute and memory with isolation enforced in hardware3. Language and task variants of the same base language model were rebuilt as LoRA adapters on one shared base model, where evaluations showed quality held. Offline work, such as re-embedding the catalogue or scoring listing quality overnight, moved to batch queues that filled spare capacity.

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: isolation, adapters and fixed partitions

Choosing the right kind of sharing. Not all GPU sharing is equal. Partitions give each model guaranteed memory and compute; looser sharing lets models contend for the same resources, so one model's spike or failure can affect others. We kept partitions for anything on the search path and accepted looser sharing only for internal and offline models.

Routing to the right adapter. Adapters only save money if requests reach a server that already has the right adapter loaded; otherwise servers spend time loading and evicting them. The gateway therefore routed by model and adapter as well as load, the pattern the Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension describes, where an endpoint picker considers queue length, memory and loaded adapters before choosing a server4.

Living with fixed partition layouts. Partition profiles are set per GPU and changing them means draining the workloads on it. Rather than reshaping partitions on demand, we defined a small number of node pools, each with a fixed layout suited to a class of model, and let the scheduler place models on the right pool. Reshaping happened in planned maintenance, not in response to traffic.

The cheapest GPU is the one you already pay for. Before buying more, find out how much of each one your models actually use.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Hardware partitions for search modelsLooser GPU sharing everywhereSearch latency cannot depend on other models' traffic
Adapters on a shared base modelOne full model per languageLess memory, faster to add languages, if quality holds
Adapter-aware routingRound-robin load balancingAvoids constant adapter loading and eviction
Fixed partition layouts per node poolReshape partitions dynamicallyReshaping needs draining; stability beats perfect packing
Offline work in batch queuesRun everything on real-time serversUses spare capacity without hurting live traffic
Evaluations per languageOne overall quality scoreAverages hide regressions in smaller languages

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: measure real GPU use per model before changing anything. It showed most of the waste sat in a few teams' habits, not in the models themselves. Differently: build per-language evaluation sets before moving to adapters; the first adapter rollout exposed a regression in a smaller language that an overall score had hidden. Related: Kubernetes inference gateways, GPU scheduling with DRA, AI capacity contracts and the India page.

item.title: Every key has an owner: machine and AI agent identity for a South African fintech
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a South African fintech can control the credentials its services and AI agents use: inventory, short-lived tokens, agent identities and a tested revoke-all.
item.content:encoded:
A South African investment and payments platform had tightened staff logins years ago. The credentials its software used were another matter: cloud keys in CI, database passwords in configuration, partner API keys shared between services, and now AI agents with their own tool access. After an attack elsewhere showed how quickly automated attackers turn one foothold into every reachable token, the company set out to know, own, shorten and be able to revoke every machine credential it had.

The situation

A South African platform offered investment accounts and payments to retail customers and small businesses. Staff identity was in good shape: single sign-on, multi-factor authentication and quarterly access reviews. Software identity was not. Pipelines deployed with long-lived cloud access keys. Services read database passwords from configuration files. Partner API keys were shared between several services, and nobody was sure which. Over the past year, teams had added AI agents: a support assistant that looked up account status, and internal agents that triaged alerts and drafted reconciliation reports, each with its own set of keys.

As a financial institution in scope of Joint Standard 2 of 2024, issued by the FSCA and the Prudential Authority and effective from 1 June 2025, the company had to maintain cybersecurity and cyber resilience controls, including identity and access management34. A security compromise involving personal information would also trigger notification duties under POPIA. The company's access controls were written around people; its regulator would not see the distinction as an excuse.

Why now. In late October, Chainalysis disclosed an intrusion by an actor using "offensive agentic techniques"2. On 6 November it said the attack had exposed password hashes and live tokens for all users, and it took key products offline1. The lesson for the board was simple: automated attackers find and use every credential they can reach, quickly. Industry research suggested the company was not unusual: a 2026 identity survey reported that only a small minority of organisations automate the lifecycle of machine identities5.

What had to be true

  • Known: every machine and agent credential in one inventory.
  • Owned: each with a named team and a purpose.
  • Short-lived: static keys replaced by credentials that expire in minutes or hours wherever possible.
  • Narrow: each identity allowed only what its job needs.
  • Revocable: all machine credentials can be rotated or revoked quickly, in a tested way.
  • Visible: every action attributable to a specific identity, and unusual use detected.

Architecture

Pipelines stopped storing cloud keys and instead exchanged a signed identity token from the CI system for short-lived cloud credentials. Services on Kubernetes used their service account identities to obtain credentials from the cloud and the secrets manager, which issued database users that expired after a few hours. Kubernetes itself follows the same principle for image pulls, where credential provider plugins fetch registry credentials on demand instead of storing them6. Partner API keys that could not be made short-lived were split so each service had its own, stored only in the secrets manager and rotated on a schedule.

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: agents, delegation and revoking without an outage

Agents acting for customers. The support assistant needed to look up a specific customer's account, but must never be able to look up any account. The token broker issued it a token only after the customer had authenticated in the conversation, scoped to that customer, read-only and expiring with the session. Internal agents had their own identities and could only call tools on an approved list. Every action was logged against both the agent and, where relevant, the person it acted for. See agentic infrastructure.

Revoking everything, safely. The scenario the board cared about was "assume every machine credential is compromised". The first tabletop exercise showed that revoking everything at once would take the platform down, because some services could not obtain new credentials without a restart and a few partner keys had no rotation process at all. Fixing that became its own workstream: services that refresh credentials automatically, a documented rotation for each partner key, and a staged revoke-all runbook rehearsed in a test environment.

If you cannot revoke a credential without breaking production, you do not control it. Make rotation routine before you need it in an emergency.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Inventory before toolingBuy a non-human identity product firstA tool cannot assign owners or decide scopes
Federated, short-lived CI credentialsRotate static keys more oftenRemoves the key rather than shrinking its life
One identity per agentAgents share a service accountActions attributable and revocable per agent
Customer-scoped tokens for the support agentBroad read access with prompt rulesLimits enforced in code, not in instructions
Staged revoke-all runbookRevoke everything at onceContains an incident without causing an outage
Partner keys split per serviceOne shared key per partnerA leak exposes one service, not all

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with the inventory and owners. It found credentials nobody remembered creating, and it made every later decision concrete. Differently: run the revoke-all tabletop in the first month; it exposed the services that could not refresh credentials, which shaped the whole plan. Related: LLMjacking and stolen AI keys, securing MCP servers, the 8 November tech news and where I work.

item.title: Safe by design: preparing a Canadian learning app's AI study companion for chatbot safety duties
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Canadian learning app for young people can prepare its AI study chatbot for proposed online safety duties: crisis escalation, no manipulative design, evidence.
item.content:encoded:
A Canadian learning app gave secondary students and young adults an AI study companion. Students used it for homework, and sometimes for things that had nothing to do with homework. With Canada proposing duties for AI chatbot services, including emergency measures for crisis situations and limits on manipulative engagement, the company wanted its chatbot to be safe by design and able to show it, before any rules took effect.

The situation

A Canadian education company ran a learning app used by secondary school students and young adults. Its most popular feature was an AI study companion: a chatbot that explained concepts, quizzed students and helped plan revision. It had a friendly persona, remembered past sessions and was tied into the app's streaks and reminders. Most conversations were about schoolwork. Some were not: exam stress, trouble at home, and occasionally something more serious. The chatbot answered those with whatever the model produced in the moment.

In June 2026 the Government of Canada introduced Bill C-34, the Safe Social Media Act, which would create duties for social media and AI chatbot services and a Digital Safety Commission to oversee them1. For chatbots, the proposed duty to act responsibly includes mitigating the risk of harmful content, putting emergency measures in place for crisis situations and mitigating harmful chatbot behaviour2. Osler notes the proposals also address manipulative engagement techniques that encourage emotional attachment3. The bill was not yet law, but the company's school and parent customers were already asking the same questions.

Why now. Canada's Budget 2026, released on 5 November, proposed $176.3 million over five years for the new commission, a sign that enforcement would be funded, not just legislated4. Building safety in before the rules settled was cheaper than retrofitting it under a deadline.

What had to be true

  • Crisis handled every time: signals detected on every message, with a fixed, tested response and a route to people.
  • No manipulative design: no feature that kept students engaged against their interests.
  • Age-appropriate by default, with stricter settings for younger users.
  • Tested continuously: safety behaviour checked whenever the model, prompts or features change.
  • Evidence on hand: a written safety plan and records that show it works.
  • Privacy respected: conversation data kept only as far as safety needs, under Canada's privacy laws.

Architecture

All model calls went through a gateway that applied policy before and after the model. A dedicated crisis detector ran on every user message, separate from the general content checks, because the cost of missing a crisis is different from the cost of missing an off-topic question. When it fired, the gateway did not call the study model at all. It returned a fixed response, reviewed by clinicians the company worked with, that acknowledged the student and gave crisis resources, including Canada's 9-8-8 helpline, then offered to continue only if the student wanted to.

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: crisis handling and engagement design

Not missing, not over-blocking. A detector tuned too loosely misses students who need help; tuned too tightly, it interrupts a student revising a history essay about war or a novel about grief. We built evaluation sets from reviewed conversations, written with clinicians and teachers, covering clear crises, ambiguous messages and schoolwork that only looks alarming. Every change to the detector, model or prompts ran against them, and misses were treated as serious defects. See evaluation sets that predict production.

Reviewing conversations without over-collecting. Reviewers needed to see what the student said and what the companion replied, as a trace with prompts and outputs, which OpenTelemetry's generative AI conventions make possible to capture as opt-in content5. Conversation content was captured only for flagged cases and samples for evaluation, stored separately with short retention and access logged, rather than logging everything by default; see LLM observability with OpenTelemetry.

Taking manipulation out. The harder conversation was about engagement. The companion had been tuned to keep sessions going, and some streak reminders used guilt ("your companion misses you"). We reviewed every engagement feature against one question: does this serve the student's learning, or only our retention numbers? Guilt-based messages went, the persona stopped expressing feelings about the student's absence, and late-night nudges were switched off for younger users.

A chatbot for young people should be judged by what it does on its worst conversation, not its average one. Design for that conversation first.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Separate crisis detector before the modelRely on the model's own safety behaviourHolds when the model or prompt changes
Fixed, clinician-reviewed crisis responseLet the model respond with careNo improvising in the highest-risk moment
Evaluation sets including schoolwork that looks alarmingCrisis examples onlyMeasures over-blocking as well as misses
Remove guilt-based engagementKeep and soften wordingRetention is not worth emotional pressure on young users
Capture content only for flagged and sampled casesLog every conversationEnough for safety, less exposure for students
Build before the bill passesWait for final rulesThe core measures make sense under any version

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: put the crisis path outside the model. It meant model upgrades never put the most important behaviour at risk. Differently: involve teachers in building evaluation sets from the start; they knew exactly which schoolwork topics would trip a detector. Related: New York's youth chatbot law, prompt injection defence, the curriculum-grounded tutor case study, the 7 November tech news and where I work.

item.title: Clock-ready: Cyber Resilience Act vulnerability handling for a German industrial software maker, as AI-found reports surge
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a German industrial software maker can meet EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting duties as AI-found vulnerability reports surge: triage, SBOMs and signed fixes.
item.content:encoded:
A German company sold machine-monitoring software to manufacturers across Europe: an edge gateway installed in factories and a cloud application. From September 2026 the EU Cyber Resilience Act required it to report actively exploited vulnerabilities on tight deadlines. At the same time, vulnerability reports were arriving faster, many of them written with AI. The company needed a product security process that could separate signal from noise, know which customers were exposed and start the regulatory clock at the right moment.

The situation

A German software company sold machine-monitoring software to manufacturers across Europe. Its product had two parts: an edge gateway installed on factory networks that collected data from machines, and a cloud application where customers viewed dashboards and alerts. Both were built on many open-source components. Security reports came in through a shared email address, were picked up by whichever engineer had time, and were tracked in the general bug tracker. Nobody could quickly say which customers ran which gateway release, or which releases contained a given library.

The product counted as a product with digital elements under the EU Cyber Resilience Act. From 11 September 2026, manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents, once, through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform, which passes them to the relevant national CSIRT and ENISA12. The first step is an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of active exploitation, followed by a fuller notification and a final report2. An email inbox and goodwill could not meet those deadlines reliably.

Why now. Vulnerability reports were getting more numerous and harder to judge. On 5 November 2026 OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber, a model for authorised vulnerability research that it rates at its highest cybersecurity risk level3. OpenAI's own security leadership has said AI-generated reports are overwhelming some open-source maintainers4, and projects such as Debian have begun experimenting with AI-assisted triage to cope5. The company was seeing the same pattern at its own scale: more reports, some excellent, many duplicated or unreproducible.

What had to be true

  • One way in: every report, from researchers, customers, suppliers or internal scanners, reaches one queue with an owner.
  • Noise filtered cheaply, without letting a real vulnerability sit unread.
  • Exposure answerable fast: for any component, which releases contain it and which customers run them.
  • A consistent start to the clock: a written rule for when the company is "aware" of active exploitation.
  • Fixes customers can trust: signed releases and advisories that say what to do.
  • Evidence kept: who knew what, when, and what was reported.

Architecture

The core was a security case record, separate from the general bug tracker, with restricted access. Every report became a case with an owner, a status and a timeline. The build pipeline produced a CycloneDX SBOM for every gateway and cloud release, and the licensing system already knew which customer ran which gateway release, so joining the two gave a direct answer to "who is exposed?". When a vulnerable library was present but its vulnerable code was not reachable, the team published a VEX statement saying so, which cut down repeated questions from customers' scanners.

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: AI triage and the start of the clock

Treating reports as untrusted input. Using a language model to read incoming reports helped with volume, but reports are written by strangers, and some could contain instructions aimed at the model. The triage model therefore had no tools, no access to code or customer data, and only produced a structured summary: claimed component, claimed impact, duplicate candidates and missing information. It could not close a case. Anything it marked as low quality still had a person glance at it before closing. See prompt injection defence for agents.

Defining "aware". The 24-hour early warning runs from when the manufacturer becomes aware of active exploitation1. A report that a flaw exists is not the same as evidence that someone is exploiting it. With the company's lawyers, we wrote a short rule: credible evidence of exploitation, such as a customer incident, a national CERT notice, a public exploit used in attacks or an entry in an exploited-vulnerability catalogue, starts the clock, and the on-call lead records the time and the evidence. Borderline cases went to a named second person within working hours, with a bias toward reporting early.

Shipping fixes to factories. Gateways sat on factory networks where customers controlled update timing. Signed releases, verifiable before installation, meant customers' operations teams could accept updates without a call to the vendor6. Advisories listed affected versions, the fixed version and a workaround for sites that could not update immediately.

Regulation sets the deadline; your inventory decides whether you can meet it. If you cannot say who runs which release, no process can report on time.

How it ran

A tabletop exercise, run before any real case, walked through a mock exploited vulnerability from report to final submission. It found gaps that documents had hidden: who held access to the reporting platform at weekends, and which customer contacts were out of date.

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Separate security case recordGeneral bug trackerRestricted access and a clean timeline for reporting
AI sorts, people decideAI closes low-quality reportsA missed real vulnerability costs far more than review time
Triage model with no tools or data accessAgent that inspects codeReports are untrusted input
Written exploitation rule agreed with legalJudgement case by caseThe clock starts consistently and defensibly
SBOM joined to customer inventorySBOM files on their ownAnswers "who is exposed?", not just "what is inside?"
Signed releases with advisoriesRelease notes onlyFactory teams can verify and act without a call

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: build the release-to-customer map before anything else. It turned every later question from an investigation into a lookup. Differently: run the tabletop exercise in the first weeks, not after the process was written; it would have shaped the runbook rather than corrected it. Related: defender-first AI models and vulnerability management, AI model supply chain security, the 6 November tech news and the Europe page.

item.title: Capacity you can move: multi-region AI serving for a US SaaS company when data centres stall
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a US B2B SaaS company can keep AI features fast and affordable when GPU capacity is tight and local opposition slows new data centres: portable, multi-region serving.
item.content:encoded:
A US B2B software company had built AI features that customers now relied on daily. Its model serving sat in one cloud region with one provider, on capacity that was hard to expand. With demand for AI compute outrunning supply and voters pushing back on new data centres, the company needed AI capacity it could move, without rebuilding the product each time.

The situation

A US software company sold a workflow platform to mid-sized businesses. Over two years it added AI features: summarising records, drafting replies, extracting data from documents and an assistant inside the product. Customers adopted them quickly. The company served open-weight models on GPUs in one cloud region, with a managed model API for a few tasks. As usage grew, adding GPU capacity in that region became slow and uncertain, and latency spiked whenever demand peaked.

Why now. Demand for AI compute was running ahead of supply: Fortune reported Microsoft's CFO saying demand for its cloud still exceeded supply3. New capacity was arriving on long timelines and through complex financing, such as Google's credit backstop for Anthropic's Kentucky data centre lease4. And in the 3 November 2026 midterms, voters sided against data centres in 40 of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, according to CNBC's analysis1, a sign of growing opposition to new AI infrastructure2. The board's question was simple: what happens to our AI features if we cannot get more capacity where we are?

What had to be true

  • No single point of capacity: AI features served from more than one region and provider.
  • Moving traffic is configuration, not a code change or a rebuild.
  • Customer data rules respected: some customers required US-only processing; some required specific providers.
  • Costs visible per feature and per customer, so capacity decisions follow value.
  • Quality held when traffic moves between models or providers.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: moving traffic without changing behaviour

Routing is easy to draw and hard to trust. A summary from one model in one region should not read differently from a summary produced somewhere else. The team built a small evaluation set for each AI feature from real, consented examples, and ran it against every model and provider combination the gateway was allowed to use. A route was only enabled for a feature when it passed that feature's evaluation; see evaluation sets that predict production.

The second difficulty was operations. Running identical clusters in two regions doubles the surface area unless they are managed as one. All clusters were built from the same infrastructure code, ran the same serving stack, and were operated from a single multi-cluster view, so engineers could see and act on every region from one place5.

Customer data rules shaped routing as much as capacity did. Some contracts required US-only processing or excluded certain providers. Those rules lived in a per-customer policy the gateway checked on every request, so overflow never sent a restricted customer's data somewhere it should not go. See Kubernetes inference gateway and model routing.

Capacity you cannot move is a dependency you cannot manage. Make moving cheap: same code, same clusters, same evaluations, different place.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Primary plus secondary regionActive-active everywhereResilience without doubling cost
Managed APIs as overflowSelf-host all capacityAbsorbs peaks without buying idle GPUs
Routes enabled per feature after evaluationRoute anywhere with capacityQuality stays consistent when traffic moves
Per-customer data policy in the gatewayRules in each featureOne place to enforce contracts
Cost per feature and customerTotal AI spend onlyCapacity follows value

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: start with per-request telemetry. It showed that a few features drove most of the cost, which changed the whole capacity plan. Differently: write customer data rules into the gateway before adding the second region; retrofitting them slowed the rollout. Related: planning around the AI capacity crunch, AI cost allocation, the 5 November tech news and the US page.

item.title: Same assistant, different model: launching an AI shopping assistant in China for a foreign consumer brand
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a foreign consumer brand can launch an AI shopping assistant in China: a locally filed model, in-country data, PIPL transfer rules and one shared codebase.
item.content:encoded:
A European consumer brand had an AI shopping assistant that answered product questions and built routines for customers in Europe and the US. China was its fastest-growing market, and the global assistant could not simply be switched on there. The task was to launch a Chinese edition that met local rules, ran on a locally permitted model and kept customer data in China, without forking the product.

The situation

A European skincare and personal care brand sold online and through partners in Europe, the US and China. Its AI shopping assistant answered questions about ingredients and products, built routines from a short questionnaire and handed off to customer service when needed. It ran on a global model provider, with logs and customer profiles in the brand's European cloud. China had its own app, mini-programme and marketplace stores, but no assistant.

Why now. On 31 October 2026, Apple and Alibaba said Alibaba's Qwen will power the China edition of Apple Intelligence, a clear signal that even global platforms ship a different model in China to meet local rules1. China's Interim Measures for generative AI services require qualifying public-facing services to go through filing with the Cyberspace Administration of China2, which publishes lists of filed services in batches3. And the Personal Information Protection Law governs any transfer of Chinese customers' data abroad, with certification measures in effect from 1 January 2026 alongside the standard contract and security assessment routes4. The brand's leadership wanted a Chinese edition for the next sales season, built the right way.

What had to be true

  • A locally permitted model for Chinese users, with the application registered where required.
  • Personal data stays in China: prompts, answers, profiles and logs.
  • One product, not two: shared code and features, with market-specific configuration.
  • Chinese-language quality proven on a local evaluation set before launch.
  • Documentation that follows the design: filing, impact assessment and transfer analysis drawn from the architecture.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: one product, two data worlds

The tempting path was a separate Chinese build: copy the code, swap the model, deploy in China. That would have doubled every future feature and fix. Instead the team moved the product to a task-level AI interface. The application asks for "answer a product question" or "build a routine", and a router decides which model serves it, based on the user's market. Prompts and safety rules became configuration per market, so Chinese prompts could reflect local language, product names and expectations without forking code. See designing AI products with a model per market.

Data was the second half. Product catalogue data is not personal, so it is synced into China. Customer profiles, conversations and logs are created and stored in China and never leave. Telemetry was the easiest thing to get wrong: the global observability stack would have pulled Chinese traces out of the country by default. The team ran a separate telemetry pipeline inside the China environment, using a shared collector with separate pipelines per channel to keep operations simple5, and only aggregated, non-personal metrics are reported to the global dashboard.

Keeping personal data in China also simplified the legal work. With nothing personal designed to leave the country, the assistant did not rely on any of PIPL's transfer mechanisms, a position counsel reviewed, and the impact assessment could describe a clean boundary rather than a set of exceptions4.

Design the boundary first and the paperwork follows. Bolt on compliance after launch and the paperwork becomes the design.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Task-level interface and routerFork the product for ChinaOne codebase, features ship to both
Locally filed model via a Chinese providerUse the global model in ChinaFits the filing regime and local expectations
Personal data stays in ChinaCentral profiles with transfer paperworkSimpler legal position and lower risk
Separate in-country telemetryGlobal observability stackTraces carry personal data; they stay local
Chinese evaluation set before launchTranslate the English testsQuality depends on local language and products

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: refactor to a task-level interface before building the China region. It turned a risky fork into configuration. Differently: build the Chinese evaluation set with the China customer service team from day one; their real questions were the best test material. Related: model routing, evaluation sets that predict production, consent-aware data in India and where I work.

item.title: Agents that advise, engineers who decide: AI for maintenance planning at a Saudi industrial operator
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Saudi industrial operator can use AI agents to plan maintenance from equipment data, hosted in-Kingdom, with an asset graph, read-only tools and engineer sign-off.
item.content:encoded:
A Saudi industrial operator had decades of equipment history, a work-order system, sensor data from its plants and a backlog of maintenance decisions waiting on scarce senior engineers. AI agents could read all of it faster than any team. The challenge was to let them help without letting them touch the plant, and to keep the data in the Kingdom.

The situation

An industrial operator in Saudi Arabia ran several processing plants. Maintenance planning depended on a small group of senior engineers who knew the equipment's history, read sensor trends, checked past work orders and decided what to fix, when and with which spares. Their backlog grew every quarter. Data was everywhere: plant historians, a work-order system, inspection reports and spreadsheets of spares, but connecting it for one decision took days.

Why now. Large Gulf industrial companies are moving AI agents into core operations. On 1 November 2026, Aramco and the Public Investment Fund closed a deal giving Aramco 49% of HUMAIN, with Aramco planning to use HUMAIN's AI infrastructure for industrial applications1. A day later, ADNOC announced it would run AI agents on OpenAI's Frontier platform across its operations, hosted on UAE-based infrastructure with human oversight of consequential decisions2. The operator's board wanted the same benefits, with clear limits on what agents could do and where data would live, under Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law34.

What had to be true

  • Agents never touch the plant. No connection to control systems; read-only access to copies of data.
  • One connected view of assets: equipment, relationships, history and spares, current and as at any past date.
  • Every recommendation carries its evidence, so an engineer can check it quickly.
  • Engineers decide. Agents draft; approved changes become normal work orders.
  • Data in the Kingdom, including the personal data in work orders and shift logs.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: giving agents the plant's context, safely

A maintenance recommendation is only as good as its context: what this pump is connected to, how it has behaved, what failed last time and whether the spare is on site. That context was spread across systems that did not agree on names. The team built an asset knowledge graph from an event log rather than from periodic copies. The OpenTelemetry community describes the same pattern for infrastructure: producers emit entity events into a durable, event-sourced log, a live graph is rebuilt from it with full history, and both people and AI assistants query it, the latter through an MCP server5.

Because the graph records when facts were true, an agent can ask what the plant looked like before a past failure, not only what it looks like now. And because agents reach the graph only through read-only MCP tools, with no route back into the plant, the worst a misbehaving agent can do is draft a poor recommendation that an engineer rejects. See entity resolution for knowledge graphs and securing MCP servers.

In industrial settings, the safest agent is one that cannot act. Give it rich context and no levers; let engineers pull the levers.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
One-way export from OTAgents query plant systems directlyNo path from AI back into control systems
Event log feeding a graphNightly copies into a warehouseCurrent state and full history in one model
Read-only MCP toolsAgents with write accessBad drafts get rejected; no bad actions happen
Recommendations, not actionsAgents raise work ordersEngineers stay accountable for the plant
In-Kingdom hostingOverseas model endpointsSimpler PDPL position and board comfort

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: record why engineers rejected or edited recommendations. Those reasons were the best training material for better tools and prompts. Differently: start the asset model with the reliability engineers on day one; naming and relationships were the slowest part to agree. Related: an energy asset knowledge graph, when agents become the user, the 3 November tech news and the Saudi Arabia page.

item.title: Every script runs as the user: locking down third-party code on an Indonesian e-wallet's web app
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an Indonesian e-wallet can stop third-party scripts acting with users' sessions: script inventory, a backend-for-frontend, CSP, integrity checks and step-up.
item.content:encoded:
An Indonesian e-wallet's web app loaded a long list of third-party scripts for analytics, chat, performance and marketing, all running with the signed-in user's authority on pages that could move money. When a hijacked performance script drained traders on another platform in October 2026, the team asked the obvious question: what could our scripts do with our users' sessions? The answer led to a new front-end architecture.

The situation

An e-wallet in Indonesia served users through a mobile app and a web app. The web app let users top up, pay merchants, transfer to bank accounts and withdraw. Over the years, marketing, product and support had added scripts from analytics providers, a tag manager, a chat widget, a session recorder, a performance monitor and several advertising pixels. Most loaded on every page, including the transfer and withdrawal flows, and several were loaded directly from vendors' servers.

Why now. On 29 October 2026, malicious code replaced a third-party performance script loaded by Polymarket's website and used signed-in traders' sessions to withdraw funds; Polymarket put the loss at about $2.7 million12. No passwords or keys were needed: the script simply acted with the access the open page already had1. The card side of the business was already subject to PCI DSS v4 requirements that scripts on payment pages be authorised and protected from tampering, and that changes to payment pages be detected3, and Indonesia's Personal Data Protection Law applies to the personal data those scripts could see4. The board wanted the risk removed, not just documented.

What had to be true

  • No third-party code on money-moving pages.
  • Every remaining script known, justified and integrity-checked, served from the e-wallet's own domain.
  • The browser holds as little power as possible: no long-lived tokens, no direct calls to vendors.
  • A live session is not enough to move money: transfers and withdrawals need fresh confirmation.
  • Changes are noticed: unexpected scripts or header changes on sensitive pages raise alerts.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: taking scripts away from the teams that rely on them

Every script had an owner who needed it: marketing measured campaigns, support used the chat widget, product watched session recordings. Simply deleting them would have failed politically and practically. The team ran an inventory first, recording for each script what it did, who owned it, which pages it loaded on and what data it could read. Many turned out to duplicate each other or to have no current owner.

The bigger change was architectural. The web app moved to a backend-for-frontend: the browser talks only to the e-wallet's own server layer, which holds session tokens and calls internal services and vendors on the user's behalf. The OpenTelemetry demo's front-end shows the same shape: client-side code calls the app's own API routes, which then call the backend services5. With that in place, analytics and marketing events could be sent server-side, so most tags no longer needed to run in the browser at all.

For the scripts that remained, such as the chat widget on help pages, the team self-hosted pinned versions with integrity hashes, so a change at the vendor could not silently change the code running in users' browsers, and listed every allowed source in a Content Security Policy with violation reporting turned on. Vendor updates became a deliberate change, reviewed like any other dependency.

Treat every third-party script as a contractor with your user's keys. Keep contractors off the floor where money moves, and check the ones you keep every time they change.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
No third-party scripts on money pagesMonitor them closelyRemoval beats detection where money moves
Backend-for-frontendBrowser calls services and vendors directlyTokens and integrations stay server-side
Server-side analyticsBrowser tagsSame insight, far less code in the page
Self-hosted, integrity-checked scriptsLoad from vendor serversVendor compromise cannot change running code
Fresh confirmation per transferTrust the active sessionA hijacked session alone cannot move money

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: strip the money pages in week one. It removed most of the risk before the longer re-architecture began. Differently: run the Content Security Policy in report-only mode from the first day of the inventory; its reports found scripts that nobody had listed. Related: architecture lessons from the Binance hack, the 2 November tech news, securing AI coding tools and where I work.

item.title: Fast tools, short leashes: securing AI coding assistants and developer machines at a UAE software house
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a UAE software house serving banks and government can secure AI coding assistants, editor extensions and API keys after a month of developer-tool attacks.
item.content:encoded:
A software house in the UAE built systems for banks and government entities, and its engineers had adopted AI coding assistants, AI-native editors and a long tail of extensions. Then October 2026 showed how attackers use exactly those tools: a backdoored coding extension in an editor marketplace, and a run of breaches at AI developer platforms feeding a market in stolen model keys. The firm needed to keep the productivity and remove the blast radius.

The situation

A software house based in the UAE built and ran systems for banks, insurers and government entities across the Gulf. Its engineers had embraced AI: coding assistants in their editors, AI-native editors with their own extension marketplaces, hosted AI development platforms for experiments, and personal API keys for several model providers. Developers had local admin rights, long-lived cloud credentials and, in some cases, access to client environments from their laptops.

Why now. October 2026 made the risk concrete. On 29 October, tampered versions of the Claude Code extension were listed in Cursor's extension marketplace for a few hours; Microsoft's analysis describes a loader that tried to add an attacker SSH key and open a reverse tunnel on developer machines12. Days earlier, a Wiz Research report described a month of breaches at AI developer platforms, with stolen AI credentials feeding LLMjacking, the resale of model access3. For a firm whose clients sit under the UAE's tightening expectations on cyber resilience and supply-chain security4, "a developer's editor was compromised" could not be allowed to mean "a client was compromised".

What had to be true

  • Only approved extensions and tools on developer machines, updated deliberately rather than automatically.
  • No long-lived secrets on laptops: nothing on a developer machine that can reach production or a client on its own.
  • One governed route to AI models, with per-team keys, limits and logs.
  • Only verified builds reach client environments.
  • Productivity kept: engineers still use AI assistants every day.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: controlling extensions without killing productivity

Extensions are the riskiest software on a developer's machine: they run with the user's rights, auto-update silently and can come from marketplaces the company does not control. The Cursor incident showed that even a well-known extension name is not a guarantee, and that auto-update can push a tampered build to thousands of machines in hours2.

Banning extensions would have failed; engineers would have worked around it. Instead the team built a private mirror. Approved extensions are pulled, scanned and pinned to a version; editors are configured to install only from the mirror; and updates are promoted after a short delay and a check of the publisher's security notices. Requests for new extensions go through a lightweight review with a target turnaround, so the approved list grows with real needs.

The second control was removing what a compromised extension could steal. Long-lived cloud keys, client VPN profiles and personal model API keys were taken off laptops. Developers get short-lived credentials for the task at hand, and AI calls use the gateway, so a stolen key from a laptop or a third-party platform is limited by the gateway's quotas and visible in its logs. See AI coding policy for engineering teams and keeping secrets out of state.

Assume one developer tool will be compromised. Design so that the worst it can do is change code that review and signing will catch, not reach a client or spend unlimited money.

The last line: only verified builds reach clients

Even with good endpoint controls, code can be tampered with. The final check sits at the client environment: only container images signed by the firm's CI, with recorded provenance, are admitted. Kubernetes supports this pattern through admission policies that validate image signatures before a pod is allowed to run5.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Private extension mirrorBan extensions or allow anyKeeps productivity, removes silent updates
AI access through a gatewayPersonal API keysLimits, logs and quick revocation
Short-lived credentialsLong-lived keys on laptopsStolen credentials expire before they are useful
Signed builds and admission checksTrust the CI pipelineTampered code cannot reach clients unnoticed
Separate access per clientShared credentials across clientsOne incident cannot spread between clients

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: give engineers a fast path to request tools. The mirror only works if it says yes quickly to reasonable requests. Differently: put the AI gateway in place before AI tools spread, not after. Personal keys scattered across laptops and platforms were the slowest thing to clean up. Related: the 1 November tech news, the Binance hack: architecture lessons, hardening a utility's management plane and the UAE page.

item.title: Answering in under a breath: voice AI agents for a Mexican e-commerce marketplace
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Mexican marketplace can run Spanish voice AI agents for order calls on an open framework, with latency budgets, human handover and data rights built in.
item.content:encoded:
A Mexican marketplace took most of its customer calls about one thing: where is my order. Wait times grew every sales season. Voice AI agents could answer those calls, but only if they sounded natural in Mexican Spanish, responded fast enough to feel like a conversation, handed over to people gracefully and respected callers' data rights. The architecture had to make all four true at once.

The situation

A marketplace in Mexico sold electronics, home goods and fashion from thousands of sellers, with deliveries handled by several carriers. Its contact centre took calls in Spanish, and most of them were about the same few things: where an order was, when it would arrive, how to change the address, how to start a return. During sales seasons, queues grew long enough that callers hung up and tried again, which made the queues longer.

Why now. On 29 October 2026, Deepgram announced it is acquiring Daily, the company behind Pipecat, a widely used open-source framework for real-time voice agents1. Both companies said Pipecat will stay under its BSD licence and move to an independent foundation whose steering committee includes Deepgram's competitors2. For a team choosing a voice agent stack, that settled the main worry about building on an open framework. On the legal side, Mexico's new personal data protection law took effect in March 202534, and legal commentary notes a right to object to automated processing that significantly affects people without human involvement3. Callers would always need a route to a person.

What had to be true

  • Natural Mexican Spanish, including regional accents, background noise and code-switching with English product names.
  • Conversational speed: replies quick enough that silence never feels like a dropped call.
  • Grounded answers only: order status from the systems, never from the model's imagination.
  • A person on request, with the conversation so far passed across.
  • Clear data rules for recordings and transcripts, and no lock-in to one speech vendor.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: latency you can feel

In text chat, a two-second delay is fine. On a phone call it feels like the line has dropped. The delay a caller hears is the sum of several stages: detecting that they stopped speaking, finishing speech recognition, the model's first tokens, any tool calls, and the first audio from speech synthesis. Each stage looked acceptable alone; together they were too slow.

The team set a latency budget per stage and traced every call end to end, so each turn showed exactly where the time went, in the same way distributed tracing shows which service in a request is slow5. That made the fixes obvious: stream everything instead of waiting for whole sentences; prefetch the caller's recent orders as soon as they are verified, so the first tool call is usually instant; use a smaller, faster model for routine turns; and play a short natural acknowledgement while a slow carrier API responds.

Turn-taking was the other half. Callers interrupt, pause mid-sentence and talk over the agent. The framework's interruption handling let the agent stop speaking when the caller started, and tuning silence detection for Spanish speech patterns cut the most awkward moments. See model routing and prompt caching for latency.

Voice agents are judged in hundreds of milliseconds. Budget latency per stage, trace every turn, and stream everything that can be streamed.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Open-source frameworkA closed voice agent platformSwap speech and model providers; no lock-in
Stream every stageSentence-by-sentence processingThe only way to stay inside the latency budget
Narrow tools for order dataGive the model raw order recordsGrounded answers and less personal data exposed
Disclose AI and offer a person upfrontOnly hand over on failureTrust, and respects the right to object
Off-peak rollout firstLaunch for a sales seasonLearn under low risk before peak load

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: build the evaluation set from real call recordings before choosing providers. Speech models that tested well on clean audio struggled with real calls. Differently: trace latency per stage from the first prototype, not after the first complaints. Related: evaluating AI agents, an agent-ready travel marketplace, today's tech news and where I work.

item.title: From guidelines to plumbing: putting MAS's AI risk management guidelines to work at a Singapore wealth manager
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a Singapore wealth manager can put MAS's final AI risk management guidelines into practice: an AI inventory, risk tiers, vendor assessments and lifecycle evidence.
item.content:encoded:
A Singapore wealth manager had AI everywhere and an inventory nowhere: vendor copilots, a suitability model, generative AI drafting client letters, and agents piloted by operations. MAS's final guidelines on AI risk management made the board accountable for all of it. The task was to turn the guidelines into systems that keep the inventory, the controls and the evidence current without a spreadsheet army.

The situation

A Singapore-based wealth manager served private and affluent clients across Asia. AI had arrived from every direction: a suitability scoring model built in-house, a vendor's generative AI assistant for relationship managers, a document tool that drafted client letters, transaction monitoring with machine learning inside, and an operations pilot using AI agents to reconcile statements. Risk kept a short spreadsheet of "AI models". Nobody believed it was complete.

Why now. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) issued its final Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management on 7 October 202613. Published summaries describe guidelines that cover all forms of AI, including generative AI and agents, on a risk-proportionate basis; that put boards and senior management in charge of AI risk appetite and oversight; and that keep the institution accountable for AI bought from vendors23. Commentary reports transition periods into 2027 and 20283. The authoritative text sits with MAS4. The board wanted to know what the firm actually used, how risky each use was, and how it would know when something went wrong.

What had to be true

  • A complete, living inventory of AI, built and bought, including features inside vendor products.
  • Risk tiers that change the controls: light for low-risk uses, rigorous for client-impacting ones.
  • Vendor AI held to the same bar, with evidence proportionate to risk.
  • Gates in the lifecycle: material AI cannot go live without evaluations and monitoring.
  • Board reporting from live data, not quarterly heroics.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: finding the AI you did not build

Most of the firm's AI was inside products it had bought. Vendors had switched on generative features in CRM, document and communications tools, often by default. Interviews missed them. The team used three nets: every generative AI call from internal systems went through an LLM gateway, which logged the application and model; procurement and renewals now asked vendors to declare AI features and their data use; and a periodic scan looked for AI SDKs and API keys in code and configuration. Each find created a draft inventory entry for an owner to complete.

Monitoring had a consistency problem. Each tool reported AI activity differently, so dashboards were stitched together by hand. The team adopted the OpenTelemetry generative AI conventions as the firm's telemetry contract and checked conformance in CI, so a service that emitted the wrong attributes failed its build rather than quietly breaking reports. OpenTelemetry Weaver provides exactly that kind of live check against a registry of conventions5.

Agents needed their own treatment. The reconciliation pilot was low risk in impact but high in autonomy, so its tier was raised: every action logged, narrow permissions and a human approval step for anything that changed client records. See when agents become the user and evaluating AI agents.

An AI inventory kept by survey is out of date the day it is finished. Wire discovery into the gateway, procurement and the codebase, and let people complete what the systems find.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Discover through systemsAnnual surveysInventory stays current as tools change
Tier by impact, autonomy and dataOne control set for all AIProportionate effort, as the guidelines intend
All generative AI through one gatewayDirect calls from each appVisibility, policy and cost in one place
Telemetry contract checked in CIDashboards fixed by handReliable evidence without manual effort
Evidence from vendors by tierAccept self-attestation everywhereAccountability stays with the firm

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: put the gateway in early. It quickly found AI uses the survey had missed. Differently: involve procurement from the start. Vendor features switched on at renewal were the largest source of new entries. Related: ISO 42001 and the NIST AI RMF, LLM observability with OpenTelemetry, an agent-ready marketplace in Southeast Asia and the Singapore page.

item.title: Our models, our metal: a sovereign LLM platform for a European telecom operator
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How a European telecom operator can run open-weight LLMs on its own GPUs for network, care and security teams, with NIS2-grade controls and a hosted fallback.
item.content:encoded:
A telecom operator in central Europe wanted generative AI for network operations, customer care and security, but would not send network configurations, customer records or incident data to an outside model. Capable open-weight models made running its own platform realistic. The task was to build one that is shared, secure, reliable and honest about cost.

The situation

A telecom operator in central Europe ran fixed and mobile networks for several million customers. Three teams wanted generative AI: network operations, to read alarms and configuration changes; customer care, to summarise interactions and draft replies; and security, to triage alerts and investigate incidents. Each had started its own pilot with a different hosted model, and the security and legal teams had stopped all three because network topology, customer data and incident details were leaving the company.

Why now. Telecom operators are essential entities under the EU's NIS2 Directive, with duties covering risk management, supply-chain security and incident reporting4. Transposition has been uneven, and the Commission took several member states to the Court of Justice in July 2026 for not implementing it3, but national laws are now arriving; Austria's, for example, applies from 1 October 20262. At the same time, capable open-weight models became realistic to run in-house; on 29 October 2026 Mistral released the weights of its trillion-parameter Large 4, pitched at security teams who want to run it on their own infrastructure1. The operator decided to build one shared, sovereign platform rather than three pilots.

What had to be true

  • Sensitive data stays in-house: network, customer and incident data only touch the operator's own infrastructure.
  • One platform, three tenants, with quotas, policies and costs kept separate.
  • Models chosen by evidence: evaluations on each team's real tasks.
  • Reliable on imperfect hardware: GPU, driver and node failures must not take services down.
  • A sensible escape hatch: hosted models for non-sensitive work, through the same controls.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: running GPUs like a utility

Buying GPUs was the easy part. Keeping them useful was not. Multi-GPU model servers are sensitive to hardware faults, driver updates and slow terminations, and Kubernetes' traditional view of devices as either present or absent does not cope well with partial failures. The Kubernetes community has documented these failure modes, from device plugin restarts to pods holding devices while they shut down5.

The team designed for those failures: health checks on GPUs and model servers, spare capacity so a failed node does not halve a model pool, staged driver and plugin updates, and a gateway that retries on a healthy replica. Scheduling moved to Dynamic Resource Allocation so model servers could ask for the exact accelerators they needed; see DRA for GPU scheduling. Sharing used quotas per tenant, with security given priority during incidents.

Model choice was the other discipline. The largest open models are impressive and expensive to hold in memory. Each tenant built an evaluation set from real tasks, and the gateway routed each task to the smallest model that met its quality bar, keeping the largest model for hard security investigations. More in running a trillion-parameter model yourself and the AI memory squeeze.

Self-hosting is an operations commitment, not a download. Budget for spare capacity, failure handling and evaluation before you budget for the biggest model.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
One shared platformA cluster per teamScarce GPUs used well; one set of controls
Gateway enforces data classificationTrust each applicationOne place to prove where data went
Smallest model that passes evaluationLargest model everywhereLower memory, cost and latency
Spare capacity for failuresRun GPUs at full allocationService survives node and driver failures
Hosted fallback for non-sensitive tasksIn-house onlyHandles peaks without overbuying hardware

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: put the gateway in first. It stopped the data leaks on day one and let the platform change underneath without tenant rework. Differently: run failure drills before the first production tenant, not after the first outage. Related: Kubernetes inference gateway, serving with vLLM, telecom observability and SLOs and the Europe page.

item.title: Results, records and research: a consent-aware data platform for an Indian diagnostics chain
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an Indian diagnostics chain can share lab results through ABDM, build research-ready data and meet the DPDP Rules' November 2026 and May 2027 milestones.
item.content:encoded:
A diagnostics chain ran hundreds of collection centres and several regional labs. Patients wanted results in their digital health records, doctors wanted trends, and the business wanted to use its data for research and AI. India's data protection rules arrive in phases through 2027. The platform had to make every use of a patient's data traceable to a purpose and, where needed, to consent.

The situation

A diagnostics chain in India ran collection centres, home sample collection and several regional laboratories. Results went out as PDFs by email and WhatsApp. Each lab used its own test codes, so a haemoglobin result from one city did not match the same test from another. The analytics team copied production tables into a warehouse with names and phone numbers intact, and the business wanted to start using the data for research partnerships and AI models.

Why now. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Rules were notified in November 2025 and apply in phases1. The consent manager framework applies from 13 November 2026, and most obligations on data fiduciaries, including notices, consent, data principal rights, breach reporting and children's data, from 13 May 202723. At the same time, the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) gives patients a digital health account and a consent-based way to share records between providers4. The chain wanted to join that ecosystem properly and be ready for the DPDP deadlines in one programme.

What had to be true

  • Purpose for every use: reporting results, billing, analytics, research and AI, each with a recorded basis.
  • Patient-approved sharing of results into digital health records through ABDM.
  • One meaning per test: local codes mapped to a standard terminology once.
  • Research kept apart: pseudonymised, purpose-bound and never mixed with operations.
  • Breach-ready: detection, assessment and reporting routes tested before May 2027.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: one test, many meanings, many purposes

The first problem was meaning. Each lab had grown its own test catalogue, so the same test had different codes and units across cities. Mapping every local code to LOINC once, with the mapping owned by a clinical team and versioned, made results comparable for doctors and usable for research. See clinical terminologies and OMOP vocabularies.

The second was purpose. Operational use, such as reporting a result, rests on a different basis from research. The team kept them physically apart. The research store follows the OMOP Common Data Model, built through a planned extract, transform and load process that starts with the person and visit structure before clinical tables5, and it only ever receives pseudonymised data for recorded purposes. See FHIR to OMOP architecture.

The third was withdrawal. A patient who withdraws consent for research must be removed from future extracts, and the system must be able to show that. Because every research load is driven by the consent service, a withdrawal stops the next load and is recorded against the patient's consent history.

Consent is not a checkbox at registration. It is a record that every pipeline reads before it moves data.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Central consent and purpose serviceConsent flags in each systemOne record every pipeline checks
Map to LOINC onceMap per use caseConsistent meaning for care and research
Separate pseudonymised research storeResearch on the warehousePurposes stay separate and auditable
Design for consent managers nowWait for registrationsInterfaces ready when managers arrive
Remove identified warehouse copiesRestrict access onlyData that is not there cannot leak

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: put clinicians in charge of terminology mapping. It was the foundation for everything else. Differently: deal with the identified warehouse copies on day one. They were the largest risk and the easiest to remove. Related: a DPDP-ready consent platform for lending, a FHIR and OMOP evidence platform, India's proposed frontier AI law and the India page.

item.title: Ready for 10 December: automated decision transparency for an Australian energy retailer
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: How an Australian energy retailer can meet the Privacy Act's automated decision disclosure duty from 10 December 2026: find every decision, record it and explain it.
item.content:encoded:
An energy retailer used software to run credit checks, set payment plans, flag hardship and trigger collections, across systems built over twenty years. From 10 December 2026, Australian organisations must explain in their privacy policy when computer programs make or substantially inform decisions that significantly affect people. The retailer first had to find out where that happened.

The situation

An Australian energy retailer served households and small businesses across several states. Software touched many decisions that matter to customers: credit checks at sign-up, security deposits, payment plan offers, hardship flags, collections steps and, at the end of the line, disconnection warnings. The logic lived in a billing platform from the 2000s, a CRM, a collections tool, a credit bureau integration and a newer machine learning model that predicted who might struggle to pay.

Why now. From 10 December 2026, APP entities must include information in their privacy policy when they have arranged for a computer program to make, or do something substantially and directly related to making, decisions that significantly affect individuals' rights or interests1. The OAIC published its final guidance on 30 September 20264. Commentary on that guidance reads it broadly: it reaches rules engines and decision-support tools, not only AI, and human review does not automatically take a decision out of scope23. The retailer's privacy policy said nothing about any of this, and nobody could list where it applied.

What had to be true

  • A complete list of significant decisions that software makes or substantially informs.
  • Disclosures that match reality, generated from that list and kept current.
  • Evidence for each decision: which system, which logic version, which data.
  • Explanations on request that customer service can give in plain language.
  • No new hidden decisions: changes to decision logic registered before release.

Architecture

The data flow, end to end

The hard part: finding decisions in twenty-year-old systems

Nobody had a list. Decision logic sat in billing configuration tables, stored procedures, collections scripts and a model in a notebook pipeline. Interviews found the obvious decisions; data found the rest. The team traced customer journeys that ended in a significant outcome, such as a deposit request or a disconnection warning, back through the systems that produced them, and recorded every step where software chose or ranked something.

Capturing evidence without rewriting the billing platform was the second problem. The OpenTelemetry Collector can read existing log files and query databases through receivers, then forward everything in one format, which is how the OpenTelemetry community recommends bringing older systems into modern observability5. The team used it to turn existing logs and table changes into structured decision events, with no change to the legacy code.

The scope calls were made with counsel. Following the guidance's broad reading, the team treated borderline cases as in scope, including the payment difficulty model, even though a person made the final hardship decision23. The hardship model was also a reason for care: it informed help for vulnerable customers, so its explanations were written with the hardship team. See explainable credit decisions in Brazil for the reason-code pattern.

You cannot disclose what you have not found. The privacy policy paragraph is the last step; the inventory is the work.

How it ran

Key decisions and trade-offs

DecisionAlternativeWhy
Treat borderline cases as in scopeNarrow reading to limit disclosureMatches the guidance and avoids later corrections
Generate disclosures from the registerWrite the policy section by handPolicy stays true as systems change
Capture events from logs and databasesModify legacy codeFaster, lower risk before the deadline
Release gate on decision logicPeriodic audits onlyNew decisions cannot appear unnoticed
Write explanations with hardship staffEngineering-written reasonsClear and appropriate for vulnerable customers

What I'd do again, and differently

Again: trace from outcomes backwards. It found decisions no interview would have surfaced, such as a deposit rule hidden in a billing configuration table. Differently: start the release gate first. Two new rules went live during the inventory and had to be found again. Related: policy layers for AI assistants, ISO 42001 and the NIST AI RMF, AI provider resilience under CPS 230 and the Australia page.
